title: Sliding Window Aggregation
explain: Time keeps moving: new contributions enter the window, old ones leave, and I maintain only the aggregate over the current window. It answers 'what is the count, sum or max over the last W?' at any moment. I choose between an exact event log and approximate time buckets, and I check whether the aggregate can be subtracted.
model:
Mental model (user's note): time moves forward; new contributions enter; expired ones are removed; keep only the aggregate of the currently valid window.

Knobs: window length W, hop or precision, the aggregate, exact versus approximate. Overlaps [tumbling windows](#/sd/f/tumbling-window): an event counts in every window covering it, so no boundary blind spot.

```
time ------------------------------------------------>
          [<--------- W --------->]            expired | in window | new
```

Two implementations:

1. **Event log (exact).** Keep raw events in a time-ordered queue or a sorted set scored by timestamp (Redis). To query: add the event, remove entries with score at or below `now - W`, count or aggregate. Memory is O(events in the window): 5,000 events/s x 600 s x 40 B = 120 MB.
2. **[Time bucket counter](#/sd/f/time-bucket-counter) (approximate).** Slice W into fixed buckets. Memory is O(W / bucket width), independent of traffic, error is one bucket.

**Incremental maintenance** (add on entry, subtract on expiry) works for **invertible** aggregates: count, sum, average as sum and count. Max, min and distinct counts are not invertible: when the maximum expires you do not know the next. Keep per-bucket values and combine (max of maxima, union of sketches) or use a monotonic deque.

Uses: rate limiting, trending, anomaly detection.

details.q: Alert on more than 5 failed logins in any 60 s. A per-minute tumbling counter sees 3 at 12:00:50 and 4 at 12:01:10. What happens?
details.a: It misses the alert: each fixed minute holds 3 and 4, yet 7 failures occurred within 20 seconds. A sliding window sees them together.

details.q: How much memory does an exact log need for 5,000 events/s, 10 minutes, 40 bytes per record?
details.a: 5,000 x 600 x 40 B = 120 MB per stream at steady state. Exactness scales with traffic; buckets do not.

details.q: Which aggregates can be maintained by add and subtract?
details.a: Sum, count, and average as a running sum and count. Maximum, minimum and distinct count cannot be subtracted, because when the current max expires you cannot recover the next. Keep per-bucket values and combine them, or use a monotonic deque for sliding max.

details.q: A trending list refreshes every second from 1,000,000 events/s over 1 minute, and a reviewer wants an exact log. Respond.
details.a: Use bucketed counters, say 1 s buckets: 60 numbers per key instead of 60 million records, with an error of at most one bucket, invisible in a trending list. Pay for exactness only when the use needs it.

details.q: How does the Redis sorted-set approach work for an exact rate limit?
details.a: ZADD the event with its timestamp as score, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE entries at or below now minus W, ZCARD to count, and compare with the threshold. All of it can be one Lua script to be atomic.

Tumbling for per-period reports where each event lands in one window and cost is minimal. Sliding for 'in the last W' questions where the edge must move continuously, such as rate limits and alerting.
